extraction_text: Many elephant warriors mounted war elephants and charged toward Shikhandin's grandson, determined to kill him.

extraction_text: Warriors from various regions (Easterners, Southerners, Angas, Vangas, Pundras, Magadhas, Tamraliptakas, Mekalas, Kosalas, Madras, Dasharnas, Nishadhas) joined with Kalingas in battle against the Panchalas.
These elephant warriors rained arrows, spears, and iron arrows upon the Panchalas.
Shikhandin's grandson countered by showering sharp arrows and iron arrows at the elephants.
Pandavas and Panchalas, armed with sharp weapons, charged forward, showering arrows on the elephants.
Warriors including Nakula, Sahadeva, Draupadi's sons, Prabhadrakas, Satyaki, Shikhandi, and Shishupala's son joined the fight.
Enraged elephants driven by Mlecchas trampled and killed many men, horses, and chariots.
Satyaki shot a swift iron arrow at the war elephant of the king of Vanga, killing it.
As the king of Vanga tried to dismount, Satyaki shot another iron arrow into his chest, killing him.
Sahadeva shot three iron arrows at the elephant of the king of Pundra.
After disabling the elephant's flag, driver, armor, and life, Sahadeva charged toward the king of Anga.
Nakula, while Sahadeva restrained the king of Anga, shot three iron arrows at him and a hundred at his elephant.
The king of Anga threw eight hundred spears at Nakula, who shattered them all.
Nakula shot a crescent-headed arrow, beheading the king of Anga, who fell with his elephant.
Enraged by their teacher's son's death, Anga elephant warriors charged at Nakula.

attributes.reason: Revenge for death of teacher's son (Anga king)

extraction_text: Warriors from Mekalas, Utkalas, Kalingas, Nishadhas, and Tamraliptakas also rained arrows and spears on Nakula.
Seeing Nakula surrounded, Pandavas, Panchalas, and Somakas became enraged and charged forward.
A fierce battle erupted between chariot warriors and elephant warriors, with thousands of spears and arrows exchanged.
Sahadeva killed eight giant elephants along with their riders using sixty-four sharp arrows.
Nakula also killed many elephants with his excellent bow and straight-flying iron arrows.
Satyaki, Drupada, Draupadi's sons, Prabhadrakas, and Shikhandi showered arrows on the elephants.
The Pandava warriors destroyed the elephant forces, causing the Kaurava army to flee like a breached river.
The Pandava forces then turned their attention to Karna.
Sahadeva angrily attacked the Kaurava army, and Dushasana rushed to fight him in a brother-versus-brother battle.
Dushasana shot three arrows into Sahadeva's chest.
Sahadeva retaliated with one iron arrow, seventy iron arrows, and two sets of three arrows at Dushasana and his charioteer.
Dushasana broke Sahadeva's bow and shot seventy-three arrows at his arms and chest.
Enraged, Sahadeva threw a sword that cut Dushasana's bow and arrows before falling to the ground.
Sahadeva took another bow and shot a fatal arrow at Dushasana, who split it with his sharp sword.
Sahadeva smiled and shot arrows to knock down Dushasana's sword.
Dushasana shot sixty-four arrows at Sahadeva's chariot, but Sahadeva cut them all with five arrows.
Sahadeva blocked Dushasana's powerful arrows and shot many arrows back at him.
Enraged, Sahadeva drew a bow and shot a deadly arrow more terrifying than Death at Dushasana.
Nakula's arrow struck Duryodhana, piercing his armor and embedding in the ground, causing Duryodhana to fall unconscious.
Duryodhana's charioteer, seeing him unconscious, quickly drove the chariot away from the battlefield.
After defeating Duryodhana, Nakula proceeded to decimate the Kaurava army.
Karna intercepted Nakula on the battlefield.
Nakula accused Karna of being the root cause of all the calamities, hostility, and strife, and vowed to kill him in battle.
Karna responded, telling Nakula to prove his valor in battle rather than boasting, and challenged him to fight.
Karna attacked Nakula first, shooting seventy-three arrows at him.
Nakula retaliated by shooting eighty snake-like arrows at Karna.
Karna, the foremost of archers, broke Nakula's bow with sharp gold-feathered arrows and then shot thirty more arrows at him.
Nakula took another powerful gold-plated bow and shot twenty arrows at Karna and three at his charioteer.
Nakula angrily shot a sharp horse-hoof arrow that broke Karna's bow.
Nakula laughed and shot three hundred arrows at the bowless Karna.
The chariot warriors and gods in the sky were astonished to see Karna being struck by Nakula.
Karna took another bow and shot five arrows that struck Nakula's collarbone.
The arrows lodged in Nakula's chest made him shine brilliantly, like the sun spreading its rays on earth.
Nakula shot seven iron arrows at Karna, breaking a corner of Karna's bow.

extraction_text: Kripa took a deep breath and attacked Shikhandin's vital points.

Shikhandin's charioteer asked if he was alright, noting he had never seen Shikhandin in such distress before.
A Brahmin (likely Drona or another sage) fired deadly arrows aimed at vital points but missed.

The charioteer drove the chariot towards Bhima, who was engaged in battle with the Kaurava army.
Gautama (likely Kripa) pursued Shikhandin's fleeing chariot, shooting hundreds of arrows and blowing his conch, likened to Indra chasing Shambara.
